Tor stopped at %1$d%% and could not reach the Tor network. This is what a network that filters Tor looks like. Turn bridges on under Settings → Tor, or use the Aether → Tor mode: Tor is then dialled through the tunnel, where the operator cannot see or block it.
The engine started but Tor never reported any progress towards the Tor network. Check that the connection is up, then try the Aether → Tor mode, which builds Tor inside the tunnel.
Tor reached the network but no connection could be opened through it. Try again — or use the Aether → Tor mode if this repeats.
Tor could not reach the Tor network in time. On a network that blocks Tor, use the Aether → Tor mode: the connection is then built inside the tunnel, where it cannot be blocked.

Tor alone, without the Aether tunnel. Your exit is a Tor exit node and your traffic passes three relays, which is the slowest and the most private of the modes. Tor has to reach the Tor network by itself here, so it uses bridges when it is blocked.

Two hops: Aether connects first, then Tor is built INSIDE that tunnel. The network you are on sees only Aether’s obfuscated transport, never Tor — so this is the mode to use where Tor is blocked. Your exit is a Tor exit node.

Three hops: Tor first, then Psiphon dialled through it. Your exit IP is Psiphon’s, reached from a Tor address, so sites that block Tor exit nodes open again while your own address stays behind Tor. The slowest mode.
Tor chooses its own exit node, and a new one per circuit. No setting can pin it to a country.
How Tor reaches the network when it is blocked.
Not needed in this mode: Tor is dialled through the Aether tunnel, so the network you are on never sees it.
One per line, in the format bridges.torproject.org hands out. Leave empty to use the bridges the app fetches for your country. A line naming a transport the app does not ship is ignored.

Tor carries TCP only — in every app, on every platform. Aether answers DNS over TCP inside Tor and drops other UDP, so QUIC-capable apps fall back to TCP. That is normal and nothing is leaking: dropped UDP goes nowhere, least of all around Tor. Expect noticeably higher latency, and expect the first connect to take a while — Tor downloads its directory before it can build a circuit.

The reverse chain: Tor first, then the Aether tunnel built INSIDE it. Your exit is a WARP address — the same as plain Aether — but the network you are on sees only Tor, and cannot tell that a VPN tunnel exists at all. Use it where Cloudflare/WARP itself is blocked or throttled but Tor still gets through. Carries normal UDP, unlike the Tor-exit modes.
Fixed to MASQUE over HTTP/2 in this mode. Tor carries TCP only and WARP’s WireGuard endpoints answer on UDP alone, so the engine refuses WireGuard and WARP×2 here.
Which country bridgedb hands out bridges for. Detection asks the network where you are, which is the request most likely to fail here.
How long Tor tries the direct path before falling back to bridges. Shorten it where Tor is definitely blocked.
The address Tor must reach before the bootstrap counts as working. Change it only if bootstrap keeps failing on a Tor that seems fine — the default target is itself blocked on some networks.

Real delay: one request through each config

Real delay is measured through each config running in Xray using HTTPS generate_204. Two attempts share a connection when possible; the faster successful request is reported. A cold attempt includes remote CONNECT and TLS, while a warm request can reuse them. Core startup and the test queue are excluded. No network means Offline; failure to start the core means Invalid config; no valid 204 response means No response. A timeout does not by itself prove that the server is blocked or down. Home uses the same target and method, but a chained tunnel can have a different delay from a direct config.
